statement_record.book: Categories and functors assemble into a category. Cat has SMALL categories as objects and functors as morphisms; Cat is locally small but not small, so Set, Group, … (not being small) are not objects of Cat. CAT has LOCALLY SMALL categories as objects and functors as morphisms; requiring local smallness of its objects keeps Russell's paradox at bay (CAT is itself not locally small, so is not an object of CAT). There is an inclusion functor Cat ⟶ CAT, and Cat IS an object of CAT.
statement_record.intree: Instance Cat : Category := { obj := Category; hom := @Functor; homset := @Functor_Setoid; ... } — one universe-polymorphic category of categories, whose file header states: 'Cat is a large category, and so cannot be an object of itself … Here that constraint is enforced by universe polymorphism: [Category@{o h p | h <= p}] lives at a strictly higher universe than its objects, so the inner categories collected by [obj := Category] sit below the universe of [Cat] itself.'
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker in two independent ways. (1) SIZE: there is exactly ONE construction, `Cat`, universe-polymorphic, so there is a Cat at every universe level, each strictly above its own objects; the Cat/CAT PAIR is not built. There is no `Small`/`LocallySmall` predicate on categories anywhere in the tree, no separate `CAT`, no inclusion functor Cat ⟶ CAT, and no in-tree statement (or Check) exhibiting Cat as an object of a higher Cat. The paradox is averted by a universe constraint caught by the elaborator, which is a faithful — arguably better — realization of the book's intent, but it is not the book's two-tier construction. (2) HOM-SETOID: this `Cat` uses Functor_Setoid, which identifies functors up to NATURAL ISOMORPHISM, so its isomorphisms are equivalences and it is Ho(Cat), not Riehl's strict Cat; the faithful rendering of the textbook bare-name 'Cat' is Instance/StrictCat.v's StrictCat (Functor_StrictEq_Setoid, object equality on the nose). evidence.intree_statement: Definition Opposite_Functor `(F : C ⟶ D) : C^op ⟶ D^op := @Build_Functor (C^op) (D^op) F (λ (x y : C^op) (f : x ~{C^op}~> y), @fmap C D F y x f) (λ x y f g, @fmap_respects _ _ F y x f g) (λ x, fmap_id) (λ x y z f g, @fmap_comp _ _ F _ _ _ g f).   Notation "F ^op".
Corollary Opposite_Functor_invol `{F : C ⟶ D} : (F^op)^op = F.  Proof. reflexivity. Qed.
Lemma op_invol {C : Category} : (C^op)^op = C.  Proof. unfold Opposite; simpl. destruct C; simpl. f_equal. Qed.

statement_record.book: Six examples of isomorphisms of categories: (i) BG ≅ BG^op by g ↦ g^{-1}; (ii) any groupoid ≅ its opposite; (iii) R-Mod ≅ Mod_{R^op}; (iv) O(X) ≅ C(X)^op for a space X; (v) Mat_R ≅ Mat_R^op by transpose; (vi) (−)^op : CAT ⟶ CAT is a non-trivial automorphism of the category of categories, and a functor F : C ⟶ D also defines a functor C^op ⟶ D^op. Closing warning: a category is NOT typically isomorphic to its opposite (compare ω and ω^op).
statement_record.intree: Opposite_Functor `(F : C ⟶ D) : C^op ⟶ D^op — the second half of clause (vi), with `(F^op)^op = F` by reflexivity (Opposite_Functor_invol) and `(C^op)^op = C` (op_invol) supplying the involutivity that makes op an automorphism-shaped operation.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: only clause (vi) is covered, and only in part. `F ↦ F^op` and the two involution laws are in force (op_invol and Opposite_Functor_invol; the library's duality architecture is built so that C^op^op = C holds definitionally, which is stronger than the book needs), but (−)^op is never PACKAGED as a functor Cat ⟶ Cat, and there is no statement that it is an automorphism or an isomorphism of Cat. Clauses (i)–(v) have no in-tree counterpart of any kind. The closing warning (ω ≇ ω^op) is likewise unwitnessed — Instance/Omega.v builds ω but proves nothing about ω^op.

(identity x ↦ Some x; composition (f ∘ g) x = match g x with None => None | Some b => f b end)

Program Definition Par : Category := {| obj := Type; hom := fun A B => A ~> option B; homset := fun P Q => {| equiv := fun f g => ∀ x, f x = g x |}; id := λ _, Some; compose := fun x y z f g => option_bind f ∘ g |}.

statement_record.book: A partial function f : X ⇀ Y is a function from a possibly empty subset X' ⊆ X (its domain of definition) to Y; the composite of f : X ⇀ Y and g : Y ⇀ Z has domain dom(f) ∩ f^{-1}(dom g). Set_partial is the category of sets and partial functions. There is a functor (−)_+ : Set_partial ⟶ Set_* sending X to X_+ := X ∪ {X} with the added element as basepoint, and a forgetful U : Set_* ⟶ Set_partial. The composite U(−)_+ is the IDENTITY endofunctor of Set_partial, but (U−)_+ sends (X,x) to a merely ISOMORPHIC pointed set, and no construction can make U injective on objects — so Set_partial and Set_* cannot be isomorphic, motivating the relaxation of GF = id, FG = id to natural isomorphism and hence the definition of natural transformation.
statement_record.intree: Part : Category (setoids and partial setoid maps, encoded as total maps into option, with Kleisli composition) and Par : Category (Coq types and A → option B). The header of Instance/Sets/Par.v names it: 'This is the category PAR (also written Par or Pfn) of setoids and partial maps … Equivalently this is the Kleisli category of the maybe monad option on Sets.'
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: only the FIRST half of the construction exists. The category itself is faithfully rendered — the option encoding makes the domain of definition implicit (None = undefined) rather than an explicit subset, and Kleisli composition is exactly the book's dom(f) ∩ f^{-1}(dom g) condition, so this is a presentation change, not a strength change. But the entire point of the construction in the book — the comparison with pointed sets and the resulting motivation for equivalence — is absent.

statement_record.book: Exercise 1.3.ii: determine what a functor between two preorders, regarded as categories, amounts to — namely a monotone (order-preserving) map.
statement_record.intree: EnrichedFunctor_Two_monotone : EnrichedFunctor _2 (enrichment of P) (enrichment of Q) ↔ MonotoneMap P Q, a bidirectional theorem with both legs Defined; supported by Enriched_Two_preorder : Enriched _2 ↔ TwoPreorder (preorders ARE the 2-enriched categories) and by Proset, which realizes a preorder as an ordinary thin category (hom := R, all parallel arrows identified).
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker in PRESENTATION, not in mathematical strength: the correspondence is proven for functors ENRICHED over the walking arrow `_2` between the 2-enrichments built from preorders, never for an ordinary `Functor (Proset P) (Proset Q)` — the exact shape the exercise asks about. The gap is genuine but shallow: `Functor (Proset P) (Proset Q)` unfolds to exactly (fobj : A → B, fmap : ∀ x y, R x y → R' (fobj x) (fobj y)) with fmap_respects/fmap_id/fmap_comp automatic by thinness (Proset's hom-setoid is `fun _ _ => True`), so the statement would be a one-line corollary — but it is not in the tree. Additional caveat: TwoPreorder carries a DECIDABILITY field (tpre_dec, used in the reverse leg to case-split on whether x ≤ y), an extra hypothesis the book's exercise does not impose.

gap: The 'functor between preorders = monotone map' correspondence exists only in the Two-ENRICHED presentation (EnrichedFunctor over the walking arrow), not for ordinary functors between the thin categories `Proset P` and `Proset Q`, and the enriched version additionally assumes the preorder is decidable (the tpre_dec field of TwoPreorder).
